Tomato___Early_blight.description: A common fungal disease of tomato and potato. It starts on the older, lower leaves and moves up the plant. Badly infected leaves turn brown and fall off.
Tomato___Early_blight.symptoms: Small dark spots on lower leaves that grow into round brown spots with target-like rings. The area around each spot often turns yellow.
guidance: Remove leaves with spots and bury or burn them. Do not compost them.
Water at the base of the plant and use mulch so soil does not splash onto the leaves.
Stake the plants and leave space between them so the leaves dry faster.
Do not plant tomatoes or peppers in the same spot for two years.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A fast-spreading disease of tomato and potato that is worst in cool, wet weather. It can destroy plants within days once it takes hold.
Tomato___Late_blight.symptoms: Irregular, water-soaked patches that turn light brown, often starting on the upper leaves. In humid weather, white fuzzy growth can appear under the leaves.
guidance: Remove and destroy infected plants and fruit straight away to slow the spread.
Avoid wetting the leaves when watering, and water early in the day.
Choose resistant varieties when planting again.
Ask a local agriculture officer before using any fungicide, as treatment works best before infection.

Tomato___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this leaf.
guidance: Keep checking the older, lower leaves, where many diseases start.
Water at the base of the plant and keep the leaves dry.
Leave space between plants so air can flow.
Remove weeds and fallen plant debris around the plants.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of tomato and pepper that spreads quickly in warm, humid weather. It is hard to control once it is established, so prevention is important.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small yellow-green spots with a water-soaked edge. The spots join together, turn brown and dry, and can leave holes and torn leaf edges.
guidance: Start with healthy, inspected seedlings.
Do not handle or work with plants while the leaves are wet.
Remove infected plant debris after the season, and control nearby weeds.
Do not plant tomatoes or peppers in the same spot in the following year.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease that thrives in very humid air, especially in greenhouses and high tunnels. It usually starts on the lower leaves.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green or yellow spots on the upper side of the leaf, with olive-green, velvety mould on the underside. Badly affected leaves die.
guidance: Improve air flow by spacing plants and opening greenhouse sides or vents.
Remove infected leaves and plants and dispose of them away from the garden.
Clean tools and equipment after working with infected plants.
Choose resistant varieties and clean seed for the next planting.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A common fungal leaf disease of tomato, favoured by wet weather. It often appears when the first fruits start to form.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Many small, round grey spots with dark edges on the lower leaves. Tiny black dots may be seen inside the spots. Affected leaves turn yellow and die.
guidance: Remove infected leaves during the season, and clear all infected plant parts at the end.
Water at the soil level and keep the leaves dry.
Use mulch to stop soil splashing onto the leaves.
Space plants and remove the lowest leaves once plants are fruiting, to improve air flow.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Damage caused by tiny mites, not by a disease. They feed on the leaves and multiply fast in hot, dry weather.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.symptoms: Fine yellow, white or brown speckles on the leaves, starting low on the plant. Heavy infestations show fine webbing, bronzed leaves and leaf drop.
guidance: Water plants regularly, as dry, stressed plants are more affected.
Spray the plants with water to knock mites off the leaves.
Use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if mites keep spreading.
Ask a local agriculture officer for advice on suitable products.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease that starts on the older leaves and spreads upward. It spreads fast in warm, wet and windy weather.
Tomato___Target_Spot.symptoms: Small spots with a yellow edge that grow up to about 1 cm and show ring patterns, like a target. Leaves turn yellow, collapse and die.
guidance: Remove some lower branches to improve air flow, and remove infected lower leaves.
Avoid overhead watering.
Keep the area free of weeds.
After harvest, collect and destroy crop remains, and wait three years before planting tomato there again.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A virus spread by whiteflies. Infected plants cannot be cured, so control focuses on removing infected plants and managing whiteflies.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.symptoms: Young leaves turn yellow between the veins and at the edges, and curl and crumple. Plants become stunted and bushy, and flowers may drop.
guidance: Remove and destroy infected plants to stop the virus spreading.
Check for whiteflies with yellow sticky traps.
Spray neem, pyrethrin or insecticidal soap on the undersides of leaves if whiteflies are many.
Plant resistant varieties and healthy seedlings next time.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A virus that spreads through seed and by handling plants, entering through small wounds. There is no chemical treatment.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Leaves show yellow and green mottled patterns and can be distorted. Plants may be stunted.
guidance: Remove infected plants straight away.
Wash hands and tools after handling plants, and avoid touching plants after using tobacco products.
Use certified disease-free seed.
Grow resistant varieties.
